subject: ventures/pilot-car-escort-run-profit-calculator
professional: an experienced pilot car / escort vehicle operator (certified lead, chase and high-pole) who quotes oversize-load escorts per loaded mile with a day-rate minimum, plus deadhead, layover, wait-time and no-go charges

evidence.correctness: Recomputed the shipped example by hand (scratchpad pilot/checks.mjs, written from the formula, not the engine): fuel 200/17*3.70 = 43.53; costs 110 + 43.53 + 36 + 45 + 12 + 13.50 + 25.33 + 45.83 = 331.20; profit 118.80; margin 26.4%; needed revenue (331.20 - 13.50)/(1 - 0.03 - 0.30) = 474.17; per loaded mile 3.3870; break-even 5500/(450 - 285.36) = 33.41 runs. Engine matches to the cent. Typing the rounded lowest quote $3.39 back into the page gives margin 30.1% (revenue 474.60), so the kill criterion 'lowest quote does not reproduce the margin' holds. At the break-even run count profit is 0.000000. Against outside sources: the $1.80/mile and $450 minimum sit inside published civilian lead/chase rates ($1.55-$2.00/mile, $400-$600 day) and $110/night equals the GSA FY2026 standard lodging rate; vehicle cost per mile on the short run (fuel+wear+depreciation+insurance share) is $0.658 vs the IRS 2026 business rate of 72.5-76 cents, plausible. Two problems make outputs a user would act on wrong: (1) a cleared field is read as 0 (Number('')): clearing the minimum charge silently bills $252 and shows a $73.26 loss; clearing driver pay shows a 50.8% margin and a $2.21 lowest quote, with status 'Done'; (2) depreciation and the yearly overhead are charged per run regardless of miles or days, so the two-run comparison headline 'Run B makes $57 more' (540 miles, 2 days vs 200 miles, 1 day) depends on that allocation: with depreciation per mile at a 250,000-mile life ($0.152/mi, closer to the IRS 35-cent depreciation component) Run A is $113.74 and Run B $119.12, a $5 gap. Arithmetic right, two input/allocation paths mislead: 2.
evidence.completeness: Walked every README/index claim in Chromium (scratchpad pilot/walk.cjs, local static server): Check this run (5 headline tiles, 18-row table, notes), minimum-charge notice, deadhead share note, below-target note with needed total and per-mile quote, two-run comparison table and per-hour note, Copy as text (clipboard read back), Download CSV (item,amount rows), Save scenario then Load saved scenario (edited price 2.1 restored into #pr), flat/day mode with 0 loaded miles, Load an example, usage counters recorded and the opt-out cleared them and persisted over reload. No console or page errors; no horizontal scroll at 375 px; guide links back to the tool. No stubs or TODOs. Everything claimed works: 3.
evidence.verification: node --test '*.test.mjs' in the subject root: tests 25, pass 25, fail 0 (0.11 s). Includes a 400-case property test that quoting minQuote earns exactly the target margin in both modes and a test that every guide figure is the engine's output. Seeded 5 mutants with quality_mutate.py (test_cmd lists the three files because the tool runs without a shell): wear on loaded miles only CAUGHT; card fee on pre-minimum quote CAUGHT; minChargeCovers threshold *1.1 CAUGHT; minApplied > -> >= SURVIVED (no equality case); break-even warning threshold runsPerYear -> runsPerYear*2 SURVIVED (the 'Break-even is N runs but you expect M' note has no test). A sixth mutant (compare tie band 0.005 -> 50) also survived but is near-equivalent on the fixture (gap is $57), so not counted. Arithmetic regressions are caught; notes and boundaries are not: 3.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (184 lines), index.html module script, usage.mjs, all three test files. Pure engine, one validator with named messages, card-fee+margin >= 100% refused, division by zero guarded for break-even, localStorage wrapped. Defects: index.html:168 readMap uses Number() so a blank input becomes 0 and passes nonneg validation (wage, min charge, tolls, meals, hotel, overhead all silently zero); calc.mjs:155 the copied text's cost breakdown lists six of nine components (omits card fees, vehicle cost and overhead share; they sum to $246.53 of $331.20); nights accepts fractions. Otherwise a reviewer would accept it.
evidence.claims: Backed: every guide figure ($252, $450, $110, $43.53, $36, $13.50, $25.33, $45.83, $331.20, $118.80, 26.4%, $23.76, $14,256, 33 runs, $317.70, $474.17, $24.17, $3.39, $1008.00, $175.86, $13.53) reproduces, by hand and by page.test.mjs; 'keeps about a quarter' = 26.4%; index 'hundreds of random runs' = 400 in calc.test.mjs; 'nothing uploaded' (no fetch/beacon, tested); usage events named in the footer equal those recorded; FAQ 'most operators set a minimum or day rate' agrees with forum and vendor rate pages. Disclaimer (no warranty, not tax/legal/insurance/financial advice, not affiliated, no SLA) on index footer, guide footer, README, copied text. served-copy: no placeholder or retired origin in llms.txt, sitemap, robots, canonicals. Weak spots: the copied-text cost breakdown reads as complete but is not (calc.mjs:155); llms.txt is a one-line description. 3.
evidence.fitness: Walked the job as an operator: priced the default 140-mile short run (minimum applies, 26.4% margin, needs $474.17), raised the rate to the suggested $3.39 and saw 30.1%, compared a 420-mile two-day run, copied the summary, saved and reloaded. A solo operator can sanity-check one run and find a minimum. But a real escort rate sheet bills deadhead (often $0.75-$1.25/mi), a height-pole premium, overnight/layover pay, wait-time per hour and no-go/cancel fees, and day rates are per day on multi-day moves; the tool has only a per-loaded-mile price or one flat total with one per-run minimum, so those lines must be folded by hand into a flat price. Per-run depreciation/overhead skews long vs short comparisons. Usable with care: 2.
evidence.domain: Compared with how escort operators and trucking cost models work: revenue = loaded-mile rate with a day minimum plus accessorial charges (deadhead, pole, layover, wait, no-go); vehicle cost per mile (ATRI-style operating cost per mile, IRS standard rate 72.5-76 c/mi with a 35 c/mi depreciation component in 2026); per diem against the IRS transportation-industry M&IE ($80 CONUS) or GSA $68; overhead per working day. Matches: margin on price with card fees solved exactly, deadhead costed in fuel and wear, driver hours including waiting, break-even on contribution. Departs: depreciation per run not per mile, overhead per run not per day, no accessorial revenue lines, no per-day day-rate mode, minimum per run not per day. Example fuel $3.70 is below the EIA late-October-2026 average ($4.27, FRED GASREGW) but labelled invented. A senior operator would sign the arithmetic, not the revenue and allocation model: 2.

defects.what: A cleared input is read as 0 (Number('') === 0) and passes the >= 0 validation: a blank minimum charge silently bills the bare mileage ($252, -$73.26 shown), a blank driver pay shows a 50.8% margin and a $2.21 lowest quote, both with status 'Done'

Vehicle depreciation is vehicleCost/lifeRuns and yearly overhead is annual/runsPerYear, both per run regardless of miles or days, so a 540-mile two-day run carries the same $25.33 + $45.83 as a 200-mile day run; the comparison headline 'Run B makes $57 more' falls to about $5 with per-mile depreciation at a 250,000-mile life

No accessorial revenue: escort rate sheets bill deadhead (often $0.75-$1.25/mi), a height-pole premium, overnight/layover, wait time per hour and no-go fees, and day rates per day on multi-day moves; the model has only a per-loaded-mile price or one flat total with a single per-run minimum
Copied text's cost breakdown lists six of nine components (omits card fees, vehicle cost per run, overhead share): $246.53 of the $331.20 total
The 'Break-even is N runs a year but you expect M' warning and the minimum-charge equality boundary are untested: both seeded mutants survive
Example fuel price $3.70/gal is about 13% below the EIA US regular average in late October 2026 ($4.27, FRED GASREGW); labelled invented, but it is the default every visitor sees

verdict: A small, honest, well-tested escort-run calculator whose arithmetic reproduces by hand to the cent (default run: $331.20 costs, $118.80 profit, 26.4% margin, $474.17 needed, $3.39/loaded mile, 33 break-even runs) and whose lowest quote, typed back in, really earns the target margin (30.1%). Every claimed feature works in Chromium and every guide figure reproduces. It misses the bar on correctness (2): a cleared field silently becomes $0 and returns a confident wrong margin, and per-run depreciation and overhead make the long-vs-short comparison headline ($57) mostly an allocation artefact (about $5 with per-mile depreciation). Fitness and domain are 2 because a real escort rate sheet's deadhead, pole, layover, wait and no-go charges and per-day day rates are not modelled. 25 tests pass; 3 of 5 seeded mutants caught. Finished, not yet senior-operator grade.
